passage:
Tuesday, hostel room, 11 pm
Decided: no placements for me. I'm going for the design course abroad next year. Spent all evening "researching" and honestly I feel sorted. Read three blogs on why campus jobs kill creativity. Messaged Ankita, the senior who skipped placements and is now freelancing; she said it was the best decision of her life. Also found a thread where people called placement offers traps. The placement cell sent a mail with last year's numbers. Didn't open it, it's just propaganda. Didn't call Joseph bhaiya either, he'll only lecture me about loans. Anyway, I've done my homework. Feeling calm for the first time this week.
Francis

qa.q: Why did Francis not open the placement cell's mail?
qa.a: Francis called the mail with last year's numbers just propaganda and did not open it.

qa.q: Why does Francis feel calm and well researched?
qa.a: Francis has read several sources that all agree, so the decision feels checked and safe. What goes unnoticed is that everything likely to disagree, like the mail and Joseph bhaiya, was skipped.

qa.q: What could Francis add to make the research real?
qa.a: Francis could open the placement mail and call Joseph bhaiya on purpose, looking for the strongest case against skipping placements. If the plan still holds after that, the calm will be earned.

qa.q: How might Ankita's advice look from where Ankita stands?
qa.a: Ankita is one senior whose freelancing worked out, so her best decision reflects her own path; she may not know Francis's money situation or skills.

grounding: Shows a college student gathering only blogs, threads and a senior who agree with skipping placements, and ignoring the data and the relative who might disagree.

passage: On the evening bus from college back to her village near Hoshiarpur, Madhuri kept her phone close to her face. She had already told the placement coordinator she would sit out this year and prepare for the state services exam at home. Now she was collecting reasons. A coaching-centre poster at the bus stand read: "Selected students never waste time on private jobs." She photographed it. A cousin's forward about a topper who studied alone: saved. When Gurpreet, sitting beside her, said his elder brother had tried for three years and was now taking any job he could get, Madhuri nodded politely and looked out of the window. That night she told her mother she had checked every side.

qa.q: What did Madhuri photograph at the bus stand?
qa.a: She photographed a coaching-centre poster that said selected students never waste time on private jobs.

qa.q: Why does Madhuri feel she has checked every side?
qa.a: She has gathered a poster, a forward and her own plan, all pointing the same way, so it feels thorough. Gurpreet's story doesn't fit, so she lets it pass without weighing it.

qa.q: What could Madhuri try before telling her mother she had checked every side?
qa.a: She could ask Gurpreet's brother what those three years were like and find out how many people from her college cleared the exam. Hearing one disappointing story on purpose makes the choice stronger either way.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet feel when Madhuri looks out of the window?
qa.a: Gurpreet may feel his brother's hard experience was brushed aside, and might hesitate to share honest warnings with her again.

grounding: Shows a college student who has already chosen to skip placements saving only the messages that agree and quietly ignoring a friend's warning.

passage: Alejandro had decided to skip the graduate recruitment fair at his university in Cape Town. He was going to build his cycling channel on a video site full-time. On Sunday he spent six hours "researching." He watched interviews with three creators who had quit their jobs and hit big numbers. He read a blog called "Your degree is a safety net you don't need." He even bookmarked a comment from a stranger: "Just go for it, bro." When his flatmate Zanele sent him an article about how few channels earn enough to pay rent, he replied with a thumbs-up and didn't open it. "I've looked at this from every angle," he told her over supper. Zanele pushed her plate aside. "Every angle that agrees with you, maybe." Alejandro laughed and went back to his notes.

qa.q: How long did Alejandro spend "researching" on Sunday?
qa.a: He spent six hours.

qa.q: Why did Alejandro reply with a thumbs-up but not open Zanele's article?
qa.a: He had already made his choice, and an article about low earnings threatened it. Staying with the encouraging stories let him keep feeling well informed and sure.

qa.q: Zanele's comment at supper was a turning point Alejandro laughed off. What could he do with it instead?
qa.a: He could list the three strongest reasons against his plan and read Zanele's article before the fair closes, then decide whether a job plus the channel on weekends might work.

qa.q: What might be going through Zanele's mind when she pushes her plate aside?
qa.a: She is probably frustrated and worried, because she can see Alejandro only collecting cheers and feels her article was ignored.

grounding: A student abroad collects only creators' success stories to support skipping the recruitment fair and ignores his flatmate's article.

passage: The career cell at the college in Guwahati had a sign-up sheet for placements, and Sabina walked past it for the third time. She had made up her mind a month ago: skip placements, study full-time for the MBA entrance. In the library she opened her laptop and searched "why placements are a trap." She saved four articles. Then she messaged two seniors who had dropped placements and cleared the exam. Both wrote back, "Best decision of my life." That evening she told her friend Bhupen, "I've done so much research. Everyone agrees." "Did you ask Dimpy-di? She didn't clear it and had no job for a year." Sabina shrugged. "Her case was different." "And the placement officer?" "They just want numbers." She closed the laptop, feeling thoroughly prepared.

qa.q: How many articles did Sabina save?
qa.a: She saved four articles.

qa.q: Why does Sabina feel "thoroughly prepared"?
qa.a: She feels confident because she has read articles and heard from seniors. But every source she chose already agreed with her, so it feels complete without being balanced.

qa.q: What choice could Sabina make before the placement deadline to test her decision?
qa.a: She could talk to Dimpy-di and the placement officer, the people most likely to disagree, and ask what went wrong for those who didn't clear the exam.

qa.q: How might Bhupen feel when Sabina dismisses each question?
qa.a: Bhupen may feel unheard and a little worried, since the questions were meant to help, and may decide to stop raising doubts.

grounding: A college student searches only for articles and seniors that support skipping placements and dismisses those who might disagree.

passage: The placement cell smelled of printer toner. Lakshmi slid her thick folder across Rehana ma'am's desk. "I've done my research. I'm opting out of placements." Inside were eleven printed articles with titles like "Why your first job doesn't matter" and "Build your own path at twenty-one." Clipped to the front was a note from two final-year seniors who had skipped placements and were "doing great." "Did you speak to anyone who skipped and regretted it?" Rehana asked. Lakshmi waved a hand. "Those are people who didn't plan properly." "And the three seniors who came back to us last year asking for off-campus help?" "Different case." Rehana closed the folder gently. "This is a lot of reading. It's all on one side." Lakshmi blinked, then laughed a little too quickly.

qa.q: How many printed articles were in Lakshmi's folder?
qa.a: There were eleven printed articles.

qa.q: Why does Lakshmi feel the decision is well researched?
qa.a: She feels confident and proud of how much she has read, without noticing that she only kept articles and seniors who agree with her.

qa.q: What would fairer research look like for Lakshmi?
qa.a: She could talk to the seniors who came back asking for off-campus help and write down the strongest reasons to sit for placements before deciding.

qa.q: How does Rehana see Lakshmi's folder?
qa.a: Rehana sees real effort that only points one way, and is gently concerned that Lakshmi is collecting agreement rather than testing the plan.

grounding: A student brings a folder of articles and seniors' notes that all support skipping placements and brushes off every example that disagrees.

Week one, a Monday. Pradeep decided in the hostel mess: he would skip campus placements and prepare for a design career. That night he searched "why placements are overrated" and read five articles. All agreed with him. He felt thorough.

Week two, a Thursday. Farida, a senior who had done both, told him, "Sit for placements anyway. You can say no later." Pradeep nodded and forgot it by dinner. He messaged two seniors who had skipped placements and were happy. Their replies he saved in a folder called 'Research.'

Week four, a Friday. The placement registration closed. Pradeep's folder had fourteen articles and six messages, all saying the same thing. Farida's advice wasn't in it. When a friend asked if he'd looked at the other side, Pradeep said, "I did a lot of research," and meant it.

qa.a: 'Research.'

qa.q: Why did Pradeep feel thorough even though he only read agreeing sources?
qa.a: He felt confident and well researched because the folder was full, but he had searched in a way that only found agreement, so it felt like proof.

qa.q: What could Pradeep have done to test his decision?
qa.a: He could have searched for the best arguments for placements and saved Farida's advice in the same folder before deciding.

qa.q: How might Farida feel when she learns Pradeep skipped placements?
qa.a: Farida may feel disappointed and a little frustrated that her advice was forgotten.

grounding: It shows a student who collects only articles and seniors' advice that back skipping placements, feeling well researched while gathering agreement, over several weeks.

passage: Suraj, you want to skip placements? Before you decide, let me tell you what I did at twenty-one. I'd already decided I would skip placements and study for an MBA abroad. Then I "researched." passage:
I'm Raghav, and last year I nearly talked myself into skipping campus placements to join a friend's music startup.

I thought I was careful. I bookmarked every article about founders who dropped out. I messaged the two seniors who'd started companies and asked them, "Was it worth it?" Of course they said yes; they were the ones it worked for.

My cousin Manjula asked, "Did you look up the ones who didn't make it?" I told her they probably didn't try hard enough. I didn't even notice how quickly I'd said that.

Then one night I actually searched for the other side. A long post by someone whose startup folded, who'd skipped placements and spent two years catching up. It wasn't dramatic. It was just honest.

I still sat for placements. I'm helping the startup on weekends. My folder of bookmarks, I realised, had been a mirror, not a map.

qa.q: Who asked Raghav whether he had looked up the ones who didn't make it?
qa.a: Raghav's cousin Manjula asked.

qa.q: Why did Raghav dismiss the people who failed so quickly?
qa.a: Raghav felt excited and protective of the plan, so failures seemed like other people's fault rather than evidence against it.

qa.q: Which choice helped Raghav decide more fairly?
qa.a: Searching for the other side and reading the honest post about a startup that folded gave Raghav the evidence the bookmarks had left out.

qa.q: How might Manjula have felt when Raghav brushed off her question?
qa.a: Manjula may have felt a bit frustrated, seeing that Raghav wasn't really listening to anything that disagreed.

grounding: A college student bookmarks only success stories and agreeing seniors about skipping placements, then seeks the other side.

passage:
Placement mentor's note, Navratri week — Noor
Kavitha, final-year commerce, has decided not to sit for campus placements. She plans to prepare for a design course abroad instead.
She came to me today with a folder she called her "research." It had eleven articles about people who skipped placements and succeeded, and notes from three seniors who did the same. When I asked if she had spoken to anyone who regretted skipping, or read anything on the other side, she said, "Why would I? I already know what I want."
She seemed confident, even relieved, as if the folder settled it.
I told her the decision may well be right for her, but that research means looking at both sides. I have given her the names of two graduates who took a placement job first and studied design later, and asked her to talk to them before the registration closes on Friday.

qa.q: How many articles were in Kavitha's research folder?
qa.a: It had eleven articles.

qa.q: Why does Kavitha feel so sure about skipping placements?
qa.a: She feels confident and relieved because her folder is full of agreeing voices, which makes her feel well researched.

qa.q: What did the mentor do, and why is it a good countermeasure?
qa.a: The mentor gave her two graduates with a different path to talk to before Friday, so she hears the other side before deciding.

qa.q: How might the two graduates see Kavitha's plan?
qa.a: They might see value in it but also share what they gained from working first, giving her a view her folder left out.

grounding: It shows, through a mentor's note, a college student collecting only articles and advice that back her decision to skip placements, and feeling well researched.
